opus-5.5.text:
I try to frame it less as "Transformers versus some replacement" and more as a question about what kind of computation and memory we actually want in a model. The core distinction I keep coming back to is how the model handles state.

A Transformer is basically a model with a perfect cache. Every token it's seen is kept around in the KV cache, and at each step it can look back over all of it. That's incredibly powerful. It's a big part of why attention is so good at precise retrieval, copying, and in-context recall. But it also means the cost grows with the context: quadratic in training, linear memory at inference. More fundamentally, it's not really compressing anything. It's storing the raw history and deciding what matters on the fly.

State space models like Mamba, and recurrent models more broadly, take the opposite stance. They maintain a fixed-size state and have to compress the history into it as they go. That's more efficient, and I'd argue it's closer to what intelligence actually requires. You can't remember everything verbatim forever; you have to decide what's worth keeping. The tradeoff is that you lose some of that exact recall, and on certain tasks you can see that gap.

So I don't think the right framing is that one wins and the other dies. They have genuinely different inductive biases and different strengths. What we've seen empirically is that hybrids, mostly SSM layers with a small number of attention layers mixed in, often beat either one alone. That tells you the two mechanisms are complementary.

The other piece I'd add is that the Transformer's strengths are partly tied to how we preprocess data. Attention works really well on tokenized language, where each token is already a fairly meaningful unit. If you move to raw, lower-level data like bytes, audio, or other signals without a natural tokenization, the picture shifts, and compressive models start to look a lot more attractive. So part of the "post-Transformer" question is really about whether we can get rid of hand-designed steps like tokenization and let models learn their own abstractions end to end. To me that's the more interesting long-term direction, more than any single architecture swap.

r001.rationale: The response compares the architectures mainly by how they handle state and memory, then extends the discussion to raw data such as bytes and audio. It notes that attention works well on tokenized language, but does not frame the comparison as being within the regime of well-tokenized data.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I like to think about it is that there isn't really a single "Transformer versus everything else" question. There are a few different axes that get conflated.

The first axis is just the basic sequence mixing mechanism. Transformers use attention, which is this all-to-all comparison between tokens. And the alternative family I've worked on, state space models like Mamba, use a recurrent or convolutional view where you compress the history into a fixed-size state. And those two things have really different inductive biases. Attention is sort of a perfect lookup. It keeps every token around, and it can go back and retrieve anything, which is incredibly useful for things like in-context learning or copying. The tradeoff is that the cost grows with the context, both in compute and especially in memory for the KV cache. A state space model, on the other hand, has a fixed state. It has to decide what to keep as it goes. That gives you constant-time per step and linear scaling, but it means you're compressing, and compression is lossy.

So I'd actually frame it less as "which one wins" and more as "what is the right amount of compression for the data you're modeling." And this is where language is interesting, because language is a pretty information-dense modality. Text has already been compressed by a human, roughly speaking. So you don't want to throw away too much, and that's partly why attention has done so well on it. But it's also not the case that every token matters equally, which is why things like Mamba can get surprisingly close at the same parameter count.

The second axis, which I think people underweight, is that these mechanisms aren't actually mutually exclusive. The Transformer "block" is attention plus an MLP plus normalization and residuals, and all of that other machinery is shared. So when people say "post-Transformer," what they usually mean is replacing the attention layer. And empirically, the thing that works best right now is often hybrids, where you have mostly SSM layers and a small fraction of attention layers. You get most of the efficiency benefits, and the attention layers cover the cases where you really need precise retrieval.

And then the third axis is just the ecosystem. Transformers have had years of hardware co-design, kernel optimization, and tooling. A lot of what looks like an algorithmic advantage is really an engineering head start. So a fair comparison has to control for that, and a lot of our work has been about making sure the alternative is actually hardware-efficient, not just asymptotically efficient on paper.

So my honest framing is: attention is probably not going away, but it's also probably not the only primitive we'll be using. The interesting question is what the right mix looks like, and how that depends on the modality and the scale.

r001.rationale: The response discusses language and text as information-dense, but does not frame the comparison as applying specifically to well-tokenized data.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to separate the architecture from the capabilities we associate with it. A lot of what we call a Transformer today is really the whole recipe: the data, the scale, the training procedure. If you replace attention with something else, you’d ideally keep those other things fixed so you can understand what the architecture is actually contributing.

Attention has a very useful property: it can look back at the context and retrieve information directly. The tradeoff is that you have to retain that context, and the cost grows as the sequence gets longer. With a recurrent model, including a state space model, you’re instead compressing the history into a fixed-size state. That gives you a very different efficiency profile, but it also puts pressure on the model to decide what to remember.

So I don’t really frame it as, ‘What’s going to replace Transformers?’ It’s more, ‘Can we get the quality we want with a better tradeoff in memory, computation, and context length?’ And the answer may depend on the task. It may also involve combining these mechanisms rather than choosing just one.

r001.rationale: The response compares attention-based and recurrent/state-space architectures, but it does not mention or establish that the comparison is within a regime of well-tokenized data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to separate the architecture from the language modeling objective. Predicting the next token doesn’t inherently require a Transformer. The question is what properties you want from the model, and what tradeoffs you’re willing to make.

Attention gives you a very powerful way to look back at the context and retrieve information. But that comes with costs as the sequence gets longer. With recurrent models, including state space models, you’re compressing the history into a state of fixed size. That can make processing long sequences and generating tokens much more efficient, but it also creates a bottleneck: what information do you keep, and how do you access it later?

So I wouldn’t frame it as one architecture being universally better. I’d ask where attention is essential, where a compressed state is sufficient, and whether combining those mechanisms gives you a better tradeoff. Matching language modeling quality is one part of that comparison; memory, inference efficiency, and how the model uses context matter too.

r001.rationale: The response compares architectures for next-token language modeling, but it does not frame that comparison as applying to well-tokenized data.
